record.label: Orthogonal mask quadratics have small exponentials
record.statement: For disjoint-mask real commuting columns d_l,e_l with weighted norms at most C_a√p_l, the centered quadratic Q=Σ_l(q(d_l)q(e_l)−⟨d_l,e_l⟩) is O_sm(ρ), ρ=(Σ_l p_l²)^(1/2). The groups exp(±itQ) separately satisfy smooth weighted bounds independent of the number of parts for bounded t and converge to identity as ρ→0. Fixed-dimensional smooth field exponentials require weighted column bounds but no inverse Gram matrix.
record.boundary: The exponential statement has its own domain and weighted Gronwall argument. It is not inferred solely from a small Hilbert–Schmidt kernel or small generator.

aligned_passages.text: ### 8.3 Seeded synthesis: helper contraction and nested responses Temporarily add longitudinal seed gates $\exp(-it\sum_i s_iZ_i)$, using an independent Gaussian $s_i$ at each vertex and reusing that same variable whenever a later seed gate acts there. The synthesis theorem turns the finite classical formula into a finite word of these gates, costs and mixers. Its ideal local $Y$ rotations have $Z$ insertion $$ v_{\rm cl}=|+\rangle m+|-\rangle n,\qquad m=\sin(2\theta). $$ Here $n$ is the remaining seed-dependent coefficient of the $|-\rangle$ component, not the number of spins. Both coefficients may depend on descendant seeds. The second term does not contribute to $\mathcal E$: $\mathsf L$ puts the root spin in $|+\rangle$, and shifting the $|-\rangle$ term puts a spin excitation into a child, orthogonal to the classical sector. Thus $\mathcal E(v_{\rm cl})=\mathcal E(m)$. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, classical rotations][q-root-energy] [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Classical synthesis”][q-synthesis-statement]. There are two different approximation operations. First, seed conjugations of $X$ generate $\cos(2ts)X$ and $\sin(2ts)Y$. Trigonometric approximation and matrix commutators give the required bounded measurable masked spin controls. Sign averaging of masked $X$ flips isolates an interaction between chosen types; the cost terms commute, so this isolation is exact. This sign averaging is the refocusing method of [Jones and Knill (1999), §II, p. 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9905008v1): orthogonal sign rows cancel unwanted Ising couplings, while identical rows retain a selected coupling. The source applies it to the finite partition of seed masks. Finite commutator products then approximate the desired pointwise matrices with smooth bounds. They can be substituted after the surrounding circuit has been fixed. The local masks are measurable functions of the seed; smoothness is required in the continuous aggregate inputs, not in the mask labels. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, elementary masked controls and matrix products][q-masked-controls]. The second operation implements an aggregation. Let $I$ be the receiver region, $J$ the sender region, and $K$ an unused helper region of fixed positive probability $p_K$. They are disjoint. The lower seed-only formula $f$ excludes these regions along its cross-edge paths. With $A_{ij}=D^{-1/2}1_{i\sim j}$, the desired propagation has generator $$ H=\sum_{i\in I,j\in J}P_iA_{ij}f_j. $$ Partition $J$ into parts $J_l$ of probabilities $p_l$. Two levels of spin commutators generate the commuting Hamiltonian $$ \widetilde H_{\mathcal P} =\frac1{p_K}\sum_l\sum_{i\in I,\,j,j'\in J_l,\,k\in K} P_iA_{ij}X_jA_{jk}X_kA_{kj'}X_{j'}f_{j'}. $$ For a fixed receiver–sender edge $i\sim j$, the terms with $j=j'$ contain $X_j^2=1$; $f_j$ is seed-only and commutes with these spin factors. On helper-pinned states $X_k=1$, so their sum is exactly $$ \frac1{p_K}P_iA_{ij}f_j \sum_{k\in K}A_{jk}A_{kj} =P_iA_{ij}f_j\frac{N_K(j)}{Dp_K}, $$ where $N_K(j)$ counts helper neighbours of $j$. Conditional on the receiver edge, its endpoint $i\in I$ is not a helper and the other $D$ neighbours have mean helper count $Dp_K$. Its binomial variance is $Dp_K(1-p_K)$, so the ratio tends to one in $L^2$ at fixed $p_K>0$. Terms with $j\ne j'$ are simple paths and must disappear under partition refinement. The factor $1/p_K$ is harmless only after a positive helper mass has been fixed. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, helper generators and contraction][q-helper-statement]. Helper pinning is a statement about every helper spin in the light cone. Its finite-degree projection is $$ \Pi_{K,V}=\prod_{v\in V} \left[1-1_K(s_v)\frac{1-X_v}{2}\right]. $$ It retains the seed variables and helper-labelled descendant spaces while fixing the helper spins in $|+\rangle$. The ideal propagation, the exact Hamiltonian $\widetilde H_{\mathcal P}$, and the surrounding gates that avoid $K$ preserve this compressed space. Multiplying an insertion by $1_{K^c}(s_o)$ only masks the root label and does not impose this descendant condition. Individual finite commutator factors may leave the compressed space. Accordingly, the proof first establishes the exact contraction there, then chooses finite commutator products on the full space to approximate it. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Simultaneous helper contraction”][q-helper-statement]. The estimate controlling a growing partition is $$ \rho^2=\sum_l p_l^2\le p_J\max_l p_l\longrightarrow0. $$ At a helper root, each part supplies two commuting fields with columns $d_l,e_l$ on disjoint sender masks, of weighted norm at most $C\sqrt{p_l}$. The remaining correction is a sum of centred quadratics $$ \sum_l\bigl[q(d_l)q(e_l)-\langle d_l,e_l\rangle\bigr]. $$ Normal ordering and disjoint-mask orthogonality bound its quadratic kernels by $C\rho$ in Hilbert–Schmidt norm. The source separately bounds the exponentials in the weighted topology, uniformly in the number of parts. Smallness of the generator on smooth vectors alone would not justify inserting its exponential into the surrounding circuit. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, “Quadratics with many orthogonal columns”][q-helper-quadratics]. The helper estimate alone does not control all cuts. Put $\epsilon_{\mathcal P}=\max_l\sqrt{p_l}$. The receiver and helper corrections have weighted size $O(\rho)$; a sender correction is $O(\sqrt{p_l})$ conditional on its label. The remaining lower-formula responses have size $O(\epsilon_{\mathcal P})$. Both quantities tend to zero with $f$, the number of lower channels and $p_K>0$ fixed. There remains a response inside the lower formula $f$. A cut can pass through a descendant used to compute $f$, rather than through one of the displayed three-edge paths. The source first writes the exact difference of the affected Hamiltonian terms before applying the preceding subtree circuit. That circuit is fixed with respect to the new cut input. Exclusions ensure that the downward coefficients are independent of that active boundary argument. The resulting additive cut-response rule retains both first derivatives and mixed second derivatives: $$ \sum_\alpha a_\alpha q(H_\alpha\mathrm{vac}) +\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda}a_\alpha a_\lambda \langle H_{\alpha\lambda}\rangle_0. $$ Here $H_\alpha$ is centred by parity; no limit of the extensive zero-input Hamiltonian is required. The self-adjoint generator is obtained from the limiting time group of cut ratios. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Additive cut responses”][q-additive-response]. After substituting the signals of a lower formula, a boundary difference contains, in particular, $$ \begin{aligned} &\sum_\alpha[m_\alpha(y)-m_\alpha(0)]q(r_\alpha)\\ &\quad+\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda} [m_\alpha(y)m_\lambda(y)-m_\alpha(0)m_\lambda(0)] c_{\alpha\lambda}. \end{aligned} $$ The mixed coefficients $c_{\alpha\lambda}$ must remain even when two channels share descendants. A bounded scalar example makes the issue visible: for a shared standard normal $Q$, take $H(y_1,y_2)=\cos(Q+y_1+y_2)-\cos Q$. At zero both first derivatives are $-\sin Q$ and are centred, but $\mathbb E H_{12}=-e^{-1/2}$. The two cross terms in the half-sum therefore contribute $-e^{-1/2}a_1a_2$. Centred first responses do not remove a mixed second response. This example checks the algebraic reason for retaining the term; the cut-response theorem supplies the operator and domain justification. At the actual root there is no parent input to subtract: the corresponding unsubtracted $m(0)$ terms enter the root update. The source propagates small terminal responses through the fixed depth and fixed list of lower channels. It refines the calling sender mask while keeping those lower formulas fixed. This is what controls all cuts in a simultaneous replacement of several calls. A root-seed scalar phase may remain on helper labels; it cancels in insertions and child conjugations. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, lower-formula responses and completion of the contraction proof][q-helper-responses]. Compilation now proceeds from outer aggregations to inner ones. Reserve a separate unused helper type for each aggregation rank. At a given rank, establish the simultaneous exact contraction, fix the sender partitions, and only then choose finite commutator approximations. Subsequent inner calls use their own helpers, which remain unused. Each inner accuracy is chosen after its surrounding finite sequence is fixed. This order avoids assuming uniformity over all helper masses, ranks or circuit lengths. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, order of compilation][q-compilation]. If the resulting insertion $v$ obeys $\|1_{H^c}(v-v_{\rm cl})\|<\eta$, seed commutation and unitarity give $\|1_Hv\|=\sqrt{p_H}$. First omit the helper part of $v$, at energy cost at most $2\sqrt{p_H}$. Compare the two insertions projected off helpers; their norm difference is below $\eta$, so their energies differ by at most $2\eta$. The projected classical insertion still has energy $\mathcal E(m)$ because $m=0$ on helpers. Thus $$ |\mathcal E(v)-\mathcal E(m)|\le2\eta+2\sqrt{p_H}. $$ All projected insertion vectors have norm at most one. This completes the interface from a bounded classical formula to a finite seeded word. It uses the source's smooth gate and helper-contraction theorems; it is not a consequence of the scalar theorem or of a finite-degree central limit theorem alone. [OpenAI (2026b), §4, synthesis statement and its proof][q-synthesis-statement].
